title: Feature Selection & Dimensionality Reduction
blurb: Tests why extra columns hurt, how filter, wrapper and embedded selection differ, how to read PCA eigenvalues and loadings, and when t-SNE and UMAP are the wrong tool.

ideas.title: Selection vs extraction: interpretability and loadings
t-SNE and UMAP: visualisation, not features

refLinks.label: §15.2.5 t-SNE and UMAP: Visualisation, Not Modelling Features

questions.prompt: A dataset keeps the same number of rows while the number of features grows from 5 to 500. What happens to the ratio between a point's nearest-neighbour distance and its farthest-neighbour distance?
options: It moves toward 1, so "nearest" stops meaning much
It moves toward 0, so neighbours become easier to tell apart
It stays the same, because Euclidean distance scales evenly
It grows past 1, so the nearest point ends up farther away
questions.explanation: In high dimensions all points end up at roughly the same distance from each other. The nearest/farthest ratio shrinks toward 1. That is why KNN, K-Means and anything built on Euclidean or cosine similarity degrade. The tempting wrong answer (toward 0) describes the opposite, where neighbours would be more distinct.

questions.prompt: Which description matches an **embedded** feature selection method?
options: Selection falls out of one model fit with sparsity or importance built in, as in Lasso
Each feature is scored alone against the target with no model at all, then the top scorers are kept
The model is retrained many times while the weakest features are dropped until a target count is reached
The features are replaced by a smaller set of new columns that blend the originals
questions.explanation: Embedded methods get selection as a side effect of a single fit. L1 regularisation drives some coefficients exactly to zero, and tree ensembles produce importances. Scoring each feature alone is a filter. Repeated retraining (RFE) is a wrapper. Building blended columns is extraction, not selection.

questions.prompt: What does `VarianceThreshold(threshold=0.01)` remove?
options: Features whose variance is at or below 0.01
Features whose standard deviation is at or below 0.01
Features whose correlation with the target is at or below 0.01
The 1% of features with the lowest variance
questions.explanation: The threshold is on **variance**, not standard deviation. Features with variance $\le$ threshold are dropped. It never looks at the target, which is why it is a filter. A standard deviation of 0.01 would correspond to a variance of 0.0001, a far stricter cut.

questions.prompt: PCA solves $\Sigma v = \lambda v$ for the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ of the standardised features. What does the eigenvalue $\lambda$ of a component tell you?
options: The variance of the data along that component's direction
How strongly that component's scores correlate with the target
Which original feature the component mostly represents
The angle between that component and the first component
questions.explanation: Each eigenvector $v$ is a direction and its eigenvalue $\lambda$ is the variance captured along it. Sorting by $\lambda$ and keeping the top $k$ keeps the most variance possible for $k$ dimensions. PCA never sees the target, so $\lambda$ says nothing about predictive power.

questions.prompt: After dimensionality reduction a column called `income` is still in the modelling table and still means income. Which kind of reduction was used?
options: Feature selection, which keeps some original columns
Feature extraction, which builds new blended columns
PCA with the number of components set to 0.95 of the variance
Kernel PCA, which maps the data to a richer space first
questions.explanation: Selection keeps some original columns unchanged, so "income stays income". Extraction (PCA, kernel PCA) replaces the columns with blends such as $0.31\times\text{income} - 0.22\times\text{age} + \dots$, so no column keeps its original meaning.

questions.prompt: Select ALL reasons the chapter gives for **not** feeding t-SNE or UMAP output into a production model.
options: There is no simple `transform()` for new data with the same guarantee as the fitted embedding (classic t-SNE has none)
Distances between clusters in the embedding are not meaningful
Results change with the random seed and with hyperparameters such as perplexity or `n_neighbors`
They need the class labels during fitting, which leaks the target
They are linear methods, so they miss curved structure
questions.explanation: The chapter lists three reasons: no reliable transform for new points, meaningless between-cluster distances, and stochastic, hyperparameter-sensitive layouts. Neither method sees the labels (the digits example stresses this), and both are non-linear. PCA is the linear one.

refLinks.label: §15.2.5 t-SNE and UMAP: Visualisation, Not Modelling Features

questions.prompt: Spread 4,096 points evenly through a unit cube. The typical nearest-neighbour spacing is about $n^{-1/d}$ of the side length. With $d = 3$ features it is $4096^{-1/3} = 1/16$. What is the spacing with $d = 12$ features and the same 4,096 points? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation: $4096 = 2^{12}$, so $4096^{-1/12} = 2^{-1} = 0.500$. The same points that sat $1/16$ of the side apart in 3D sit half the side apart in 12D. Nothing about the data changed except the number of columns.

questions.prompt: You run `RFE(estimator=model, n_features_to_select=10, step=1)` on 40 features. RFE fits the model, drops the weakest feature, and repeats while more than 10 features remain, then fits once more on the final 10. How many times is the model fitted in total? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: Fits happen with 40, 39, ..., 11 features (30 fits), each followed by one elimination. The last one leaves 10 features, and RFE fits once more on those: $30 + 1 = 31$. Runtime scales with the number of features removed, which is why the chapter warns against a slow model inside RFE.

questions.prompt: Four one-hot columns are 1 in 0.5%, 1%, 3% and 50% of rows. A 0/1 column that is 1 in a fraction $p$ of rows has variance $p(1-p)$. Select ALL columns that `VarianceThreshold(threshold=0.01)` keeps.
options: The 0.5% column
The 1% column
The 3% column
The 50% column
questions.explanation: Variances: $0.005\times0.995 = 0.004975$, $0.01\times0.99 = 0.0099$, $0.03\times0.97 = 0.0291$, $0.5\times0.5 = 0.25$. Only the last two exceed 0.01. The 1% column is the trap, since $0.0099$ falls under the threshold by only 0.0001. One-hot columns share a 0-1 scale, which is the case where the chapter says variance thresholding is safe.

questions.prompt: A common redundancy check is the variance inflation factor, $\text{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)$, where $R_j^2$ comes from regressing feature $j$ on all the other features. Regressing `credit_limit` on the other features gives $R^2 = 0.875$. What is its VIF? Give a decimal to 1 d.p.
questions.explanation: $\text{VIF} = 1/(1 - 0.875) = 1/0.125 = 8.0$. The other features explain 87.5% of `credit_limit`'s variance, so it adds little new information. This is the multi-feature version of the chapter's "highly correlated pair" filter.

questions.prompt: PCA on 5 standardised features gives eigenvalues $2.4, 1.3, 0.7, 0.4, 0.2$. What is the smallest number of components that reaches at least 90% cumulative explained variance? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: The eigenvalues sum to 5 (standardised features each have variance 1). Explained variance ratios are $0.48, 0.26, 0.14, 0.08, 0.04$. Cumulative: $0.48, 0.74, 0.88, 0.96, 1.00$. Three components give only 88%, so you need 4.

questions.prompt: PC2 has loadings `income 0.35`, `spend 0.40`, `tenure 0.21`, `age -0.74`. Which original feature drives PC2 most strongly?
options: `age`
`spend`
`income`
`tenure`
questions.explanation: Strength is the size of the loading, $|{-0.74}| = 0.74$. The sign only gives the direction. `spend` is the tempting answer because it has the largest positive loading, but sign does not signal importance.

questions.prompt: A customer wants to shrink 300 numeric columns to about 10 dense inputs for a churn model. The model scores new customers every night and the transform must give the same output on every run. Which technique fits?
options: PCA fitted on training data, then `.transform()` each night
t-SNE with `n_components=10` and a fixed `random_state`
UMAP refitted from scratch each night on only the new batch
t-SNE refitted each night on training plus new customers
questions.explanation: PCA is linear, deterministic and has a proper `transform()` for new rows, so it suits reduced features that feed a model. Classic t-SNE has no transform for new points, and refitting it (or UMAP) each night gives a different layout every time. A fixed seed does not fix the missing transform.

refLinks.label: §15.2.5 t-SNE and UMAP: Visualisation, Not Modelling Features

questions.prompt: A team has 5,000 rows and 4 features. Using spacing $\approx n^{-1/d}$, they want to add 8 engineered features (12 in total) and keep the same nearest-neighbour spacing they had with 4 features. How many rows would they need? Give the answer in **billions** to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: Keep $n^{-1/d}$ fixed: $n_{12}^{-1/12} = 5000^{-1/4}$, so $n_{12} = 5000^{12/4} = 5000^3 = 1.25\times10^{11}$, which is 125 billion rows. Spacing with the original rows goes from $5000^{-1/4}\approx0.119$ to $5000^{-1/12}\approx0.492$. Tripling the column count cubes the rows needed. That is the exponential growth behind the curse.

questions.prompt: A Random Forest ranks features by importance. `balance_usd` and `balance_eur` (the same quantity in two currencies, correlation 0.999) score 0.07 each. `tenure` scores 0.11. A colleague wants to drop both balance columns as "less important than tenure". What is the best response?
options: The copies split the importance. Drop one, refit, and the other will likely score near their combined 0.14
Trust the ranking. Tree importances are unbiased, so both balance columns carry less signal than tenure does
Keep both copies. Correlated duplicates always improve Random Forest accuracy by adding votes
Switch to PCA. Importances are meaningless whenever any two features are correlated
questions.explanation: Trees split arbitrarily between near-identical features, so importance gets diluted across both and each looks weaker than a single copy would. The chapter's fix is to decorrelate first (Procedure 15.1), then read importances. Importances are a hint, and they are known to be biased by correlated features, so "trust the ranking" is the trap.

questions.prompt:
Listing 15.2's correlation filter runs on this absolute correlation matrix:

|   | a | b | c | d |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a | 1 | 0.97 | 0.40 | 0.10 |
| b | 0.97 | 1 | 0.96 | 0.30 |
| c | 0.40 | 0.96 | 1 | 0.20 |
| d | 0.10 | 0.30 | 0.20 | 1 |

```python
upper_mask = np.triu(np.ones(corr_matrix.shape), k=1).astype(bool)
upper = corr_matrix.where(upper_mask)
to_drop = [col for col in upper.columns if any(upper[col] > 0.95)]
```

What is `to_drop`?
questions.explanation: `upper[col]` holds that column's correlations with the columns **before** it. Column b has $0.97$ with a, so b is dropped. Column c has $0.96$ with b, so c is dropped too. The list is built in one pass, so it does not notice that once b is gone, c is no longer redundant with anything kept. `['b']` is what a careful sequential filter would return. This one-pass filter can over-drop along chains of correlation.

questions.prompt: Two standardised features have correlation 0.6, so their covariance matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0.6\\ 0.6 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. What fraction of total variance does the first principal component explain? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation: Eigenvalues solve $(1-\lambda)^2 = 0.36$, so $\lambda = 1 \pm 0.6$, giving $1.6$ and $0.4$. The total is 2. PC1 explains $1.6/2 = 0.80$. Its direction is $(1,1)/\sqrt2$, the shared part of the two features. PC2 along $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ holds the remaining 20%.

questions.prompt: A logistic regression is fitted on two principal components of standardised data. Its coefficients are $\beta_{PC1} = 0.8$ and $\beta_{PC2} = -1.5$. Standardised `income` has loading 0.6 on PC1 and 0.3 on PC2. If a customer's standardised income rises by 1 with everything else fixed, by how much does the model's log-odds change? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation: A PC score is the dot product of the standardised row with the loading vector. So +1 in income moves PC1 by $0.6$ and PC2 by $0.3$. The log-odds change is $0.8\times0.6 + (-1.5)\times0.3 = 0.48 - 0.45 = 0.03$. Income loads heavily on both components, yet its net effect is almost zero. You can only see that by unwinding every component, which is the interpretability cost of extraction.

questions.prompt: A UMAP plot of customer data coloured by segment shows segment A far from segment B, segment A drawn twice as large as segment C, and a small island of 40 points sitting away from every segment. Select ALL conclusions the plot supports.
options: Points within each segment tend to be near similar points, so the segments separate locally
The 40-point island is worth investigating as a possible outlier cluster
A is more different from B than from C, because A sits farther from B
Segment A has twice the spread of segment C in the original feature space
questions.explanation: t-SNE and UMAP preserve local neighbourhoods reliably. Checking whether classes separate and spotting outlier clusters are the uses the chapter endorses. Distances between clusters are not meaningful. The chapter says only local neighbourhood structure is preserved reliably, so a cluster's drawn size is not a measure of its spread in the original space either (Wattenberg et al. make the same point). So the last two readings are traps.

refLinks.label: §15.2.5 t-SNE and UMAP: Visualisation, Not Modelling Features

questions.prompt: A dataset has 12 informative features plus 40 pure-noise features. A KNN classifier and a Random Forest are each trained on all 52, then again on the 12 informative ones. What does the chapter lead you to expect?
options: KNN improves a lot. The Random Forest changes little, because trees rarely split on unhelpful features
Both improve by about the same amount, because the curse of dimensionality hits every model equally
The Random Forest improves a lot. KNN changes little, because distances average out noise
Neither changes much, because 40 extra features is far too few for the curse of dimensionality to matter
questions.explanation: Noise columns add to every distance, so KNN's notion of "nearest" degrades badly. Tree ensembles are relatively robust to irrelevant features. The chapter says selection matters most for linear and distance-based models and is not a required step before training. In the worked example the Random Forest gains under 2 points of accuracy from selection (0.912 to 0.928), which is modest.

questions.prompt: A team has 2,000 rows and 5,000 features. They rank features by mutual information on all 2,000 rows, keep the top 50, then run 5-fold cross-validation on those 50. CV accuracy is 0.91. A fresh month of data gives 0.62. What went wrong, and what is the fix?
options: Selection saw the validation rows. Put the selector in a `Pipeline` so each training fold refits it
Mutual information misses non-linear signal. Switch to Pearson correlation with the target
Five folds is too few for 5,000 features. Move to 10-fold CV on the same 50 selected features
The top 50 is too many for 2,000 rows. Keep the top 10 using the same all-row ranking
questions.explanation: With 5,000 features and 2,000 rows, some noise features look predictive by chance. Ranking on all rows lets those chance matches into every validation fold, so CV rewards them. Fitting the selector only on the training fold (a `Pipeline` inside CV, Chapter 13) gives an honest estimate. More folds or a smaller k still use the leaked ranking. Correlation is blinder to non-linear signal than MI, not better.

questions.prompt: Someone runs PCA on **unscaled** data. `income` (in dollars/100) has variance 400, `tenure` (years) has variance 0.25, and their covariance is 6. Their correlation is $6/(20\times0.5) = 0.6$, the same as in a standardised case where PC1 explains 80%. What fraction of variance does PC1 explain on the unscaled covariance matrix $\begin{pmatrix}400 & 6\\ 6 & 0.25\end{pmatrix}$? Give a decimal to 4 d.p.
questions.explanation: Trace $= 400.25$, determinant $= 400\times0.25 - 36 = 64$. The eigenvalues solve $\lambda^2 - 400.25\lambda + 64 = 0$, so $\lambda_1 = (400.25 + \sqrt{400.25^2 - 256})/2 \approx 400.09$ and $\lambda_2 \approx 0.16$. PC1 explains $400.09/400.25 \approx 0.9996$. PC1 is almost pure income because of its units, not because it carries more information. After standardising the same data, PC1 explains 0.80. This is why the chapter says to standardise before PCA.

questions.prompt: A team fits t-SNE once on training and test rows together, then trains a classifier on the 2-D t-SNE coordinates. Test accuracy looks excellent. In production they rerun t-SNE on training rows plus each day's new rows, and accuracy collapses. Which explanation is most complete?
options: Fitting on test rows leaked their structure, and each rerun gives a new layout the classifier never saw
The test set was too small. More test rows fed into the same t-SNE fit would have revealed the problem
t-SNE needs a higher perplexity for production data. Raising it would make the axes stable across reruns
The classifier overfits 2-D inputs. Asking t-SNE for 10 components instead of 2 would fix it
questions.explanation: Two problems combine. Fitting the reduction on test data leaks test-set structure into the transform (the same mistake as fitting PCA on train plus test). And classic t-SNE has no `transform()`, so each rerun is a new stochastic embedding whose axes mean something different. No choice of perplexity or component count gives a stable mapping. Use PCA or feature selection, fitted on training data only.

refLinks.label: §15.2.5 t-SNE and UMAP: Visualisation, Not Modelling Features

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in your own words why feature selection preserves interpretability while feature extraction does not, using the "income is still income" framing from this chapter.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Feature selection removes features but keeps the survivors as-is, so "income" in the output is still literally income. Its scale, units, and meaning are unchanged, and a domain expert can interpret it directly. Feature extraction (PCA) creates new features as linear combinations of many originals. A principal component has no inherent real-world meaning of its own, only a mix of loadings across original features.

bookExercises.prompt: Classify each of the following as a filter, wrapper, or embedded method, and give one reason: (a) dropping features with variance below 0.01; (b) RFECV; (c) keeping features with Random Forest importance above the median.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) Variance threshold: filter (no model involved, judges only the feature's own spread). (b) RFECV: wrapper (repeatedly retrains a model and cross-validates to pick a feature count). (c) Random Forest importance above the median: embedded (importance is a byproduct of fitting one model, not a separate model-agnostic step or repeated retraining).

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 15.3 as a starting point, rerun mutual-information selection with `k=5` instead of `k=10` on the synthetic dataset from Listing 15.8, and report whether the resulting 5 features are a subset of the 15 reported in the Worked Example.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: With `k=5`, `SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=5)` keeps the 5 highest-MI-scoring features. Since mutual information scores are computed once and simply ranked, the top 5 are necessarily a subset of the top 10 (which is itself a subset of any top-15 selection). The ranking doesn't change with k, only how far down it you cut.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 15.9's logic, find how many components are needed to reach 99% cumulative explained variance on the same 50-feature training set, and compare the result to the 37 needed for 95%.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Reaching 99% cumulative explained variance requires strictly more components than reaching 95% (variance capture is monotonic in component count), so the 99% threshold needs more than 37 components, typically several more. The marginal variance captured per additional component shrinks quickly once past the "elbow," so climbing the last few percentage points is disproportionately expensive in components used.

bookExercises.prompt: Reproduce the digits-dataset PCA vs. t-SNE timing comparison from the Worked Example, but with `perplexity=5` instead of `perplexity=30` in the t-SNE call. Describe qualitatively how the resulting 2D plot's cluster tightness changes.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Lowering perplexity from 30 to 5 tells t-SNE to weight a much smaller local neighbourhood per point. The resulting plot typically shows tighter, more numerous, more fragmented small clusters. Local structure within digit classes becomes more visible, but the plot loses some of the smooth global separation between whole digit classes that a larger perplexity provides.

bookExercises.prompt: The Worked Example shows RFECV and embedded Random Forest importance both beating the 50-feature baseline. Using the curse of dimensionality from this chapter's Exposition, explain why removing features can improve accuracy rather than merely preserving it.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: In high dimensions, many features are noisy or redundant. A model can fit spurious patterns in that noise (overfitting), and irrelevant dimensions make distance-based reasoning less meaningful (the curse of dimensionality). Removing such features doesn't just save compute. It removes the substrate the model could otherwise overfit to, which is why validation accuracy can rise, not just hold steady, after selection.

bookExercises.prompt: A regulator requires that a credit-scoring model's predictions be explainable in terms of the original applicant-provided variables. A colleague proposes using PCA to cut a 200-feature dataset down to 20 components first. Write two or three sentences explaining why this is likely to cause a problem, and what you'd suggest instead.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: PCA components are linear combinations of many original applicant-provided variables (income, age, credit history, etc. all blended with different weights). A regulator asking "why was this applicant denied" cannot be given an answer in terms of "component 7" in any way a human applicant could act on or an auditor could verify against the original variables. Feature selection (keeping a subset of the 200 original variables, e.g. via RFECV or embedded importance) preserves that direct explainability and should be recommended instead.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the Wattenberg et al. "How to Use t-SNE Effectively" piece cited above. Identify one t-SNE pitfall it describes that this chapter did not mention, and explain how it would change the interpretation of the digits-dataset t-SNE plot in the Worked Example.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. Wattenberg et al.'s piece emphasises that t-SNE cluster sizes and inter-cluster distances in the resulting plot are not reliably meaningful. Only relative local neighbourhoods are. Applied to the digits plot, a viewer should resist reading "digit class 3's cluster is bigger than class 7's" or "class 1 is closer to class 4 than to class 9" as quantitatively meaningful facts, even though the plot visually invites exactly that reading.
